title: SCD1 Inhibition Blocks the AKT-NRF2-SLC7A11 Pathway to Induce Lipid Metabolism Remodeling and Ferroptosis Priming in Lung Adenocarcinoma
author: Utsav Sen; Charles Coleman; Nishant Gandhi; Vrinda Jethalia; Deniz Demircioglu; Andrew Elliott; Ari M Vanderwalde; Omar Hayatt; Elisa de Stanchina; Balazs Halmos; Patrick C Ma; Mirela Berisa; Dan Hasson; Triparna Sen
text:
Abstract
Concurrent inactivating mutations in STK11 and KEAP1 drive primary resistance to therapies, leading to worse outcomes in KRAS-mutated lung adenocarcinoma (KRASmut-LUAD) and are associated with metabolic alterations. Elucidation of the underlying biology of this aggressive LUAD subset is needed to develop effective treatments to improve patient outcomes. Our transcriptomic analysis of 5498 “real-world” KRASmut-LUADs demonstrated that STK11/KEAP1 co-mutation led to upregulation of fatty acid and redox signaling pathways and considerable enrichment of the metabolic genes SCD1 and SLC7A11. High expression of SCD1 and SLC7A11 predicted poor prognosis in KRASmut-patients. Transcriptomics, lipidomics, and kinase arrays in preclinical models demonstrated that SCD1 inhibition promoted ferroptosis, altered fatty acid metabolism, and downregulated SLC7A11 via AKT-GSK3β-NRF2 signaling. SCD1 inhibition caused appreciable tumor regression in xenografts and augmented the efficacy of the ferroptosis inducer erastin. Overall, this study provides insights into the role of the SCD1-SLC7A11 axis in regulating metabolic programming and predicting poor patient outcomes in a genetically defined subset of KRASmut-LUAD.
Keywords: LUAD, SCD1, Ferroptosis, SLC7A11, GSK3β, AKT, Lipid Metabolism
Statement of Significance
SCD1 and SLC7A11 are prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets for KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant lung adenocarcinoma, which will refocus mechanistic studies and lead to treatment strategies for lung cancer.
Introduction
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common type of lung cancer, accounting for approximately 85% of the cases [1], [2]. Important advancements in the treatment of NSCLC have been achieved over the past two decades [3]. However, the overall cure and survival rates remain low, particularly in metastatic disease, mainly due to primary and acquired resistance to current care standards. STK11 mutations occur in 30–35% of KRAS mutant NSCLCs and are the third most mutated gene in NSCLC, and about half of the patients with STK11 loss have KEAP1 LOF mutations [4], [5]. We and others have previously reported that KRAS-mutant tumors with concurrent mutations in STK11 and KEAP1 are associated with significantly poorer outcomes, being remarkably aggressive and unresponsive to chemo- and immunotherapy [6],[7].
STK11 activates a family of 14 downstream kinases, including AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), affecting pathways involved in tumor growth and survival [8]. KEAP1 is a negative regulator of the transcription factor nuclear factor erythroid-1 like 2 (NFE2L2/NRF2). NRF2 is an important regulator of cellular antioxidant defense mechanisms including the transcription of the solute carrier family 7-member 11(SLC7A11) gene [9], [10]. SLC7A11 is an important component of the cystine-glutamate transporter system Xc- (xCT), essential for the synthesis of glutathione (GSH). Cysteine is a rate-limiting substrate for the synthesis of GSH and may be imported directly or in its oxidized form cystine via xCT [11]. Interestingly, the xCT system is also critical for ferroptosis-mediated cell death [12], [13].
Previously, reports have shown that tumors with a concurrent loss of STK11 and KEAP1 had a higher proliferative potential [14], [15] and were resistant to ferroptosis induction [4] than single mutants. Ferroptosis is a genetically distinct form of regulated cell death characterized by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation that leads to loss of plasma membrane integrity [13], [16]. The increased expression of Stearoyl coenzyme A desaturase-1 (SCD1) in this co-mutant subtype of LUAD mainly regulated the aggressive nature of these cells [4]. SCD1 plays a crucial role in lipid biosynthesis and metabolism, helping dividing cancer cells to expand their fatty acid reservoir essential for cancer progression [17].
Here, we investigate the biological consequence of KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutation on the transcriptomic landscape of a large cohort of “real-world” LUAD specimens, cell lines, and animal models. We show that SCD1-depletion regulates SLC7A11 expression and in turn cysteine/glutathione levels via the AKT/GSK3β/NRF2 axis. Our findings indicate that SCD1 depletion in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant tumors modulates the conversion of saturated fatty acids (SFAs) to mono-unsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) and mediates poly unsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) accumulation and ferroptotic cell death. Therefore, we identify SCD1 and SLC7A11 as potent biomarkers, uncover the importance of SCD1 inhibition, and underscore the importance of the SCD1/SLC7A11 axis in a genetically defined subset of KRASmut-LUADs with a particularly poor prognosis.
Materials and Methods
Next generation sequencing of DNA (Clinical data)
Between 2017 and 2022, NSCLC tumors underwent molecular profiling at Caris Life Sciences (Phoenix, AZ) and the methodological details were provided by Caris Life Sciences as described below. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) was conducted on genomic DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor specimens using either the NextSeq or NovaSeq 6000 platforms (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA). Tumors sequenced on the NextSeq platform were analyzed using a custom-designed SureSelect XT assay, which targeted 592 whole genes (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA). For tumors sequenced on the NovaSeq platform, 719 clinically significant genes were enriched with high coverage and read-depth, supplemented by an additional panel designed to capture over 20,000 genes at a lower read-depth. Variant detection was performed with greater than 99% confidence, based on allele frequency and amplicon coverage, achieving an average sequencing depth exceeding 500 and an analytical sensitivity sufficient to identify variants with a variant allele frequency (VAF) of at least 5%. Identified genetic variants were reviewed by board-certified molecular geneticists and classified according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) criteria as ‘pathogenic (P),’ ‘likely pathogenic (LP),’ ‘variant of unknown significance,’ ‘likely benign,’ or ‘benign.’ For the purpose of calculating mutation frequencies, P and LP variants were considered mutations. The molecular analysis of these samples was performed at Caris, with data analysis conducted in collaboration between the authors and Caris.
The study population was restricted to KRAS mutated lung adenocarcinoma differing on KEAP1 and STK11 co-mutation status. The study cohorts were: KRASmut/STK11wt/KEAP1wt (n=3835), KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1wt (n=691), KRASmut/STK11wt/KEAP1mut (n=369), KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut (n=603) with patient demographics being described in Supplementary Table S1.
Whole Transcriptome Sequencing (WTS) (Clinical data)
Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) specimens (n=5259 out of 5498) underwent a pathology evaluation to assess tumor content percentage and tumor size and the methodological details were provided by Caris Life Sciences (Phoenix, AZ) as described below. To proceed with microdissection, a minimum tumor content of 10% within the selected area was required for effective enrichment and extraction of tumor-specific RNA. RNA extraction was carried out using the Qiagen RNA FFPE tissue extraction kit, while the RNA’s quality and quantity were assessed with the Agilent TapeStation. Biotinylated RNA baits were hybridized to synthesized and purified cDNA targets, followed by amplification of the bait-target complexes through a post-capture PCR reaction. Whole transcriptome sequencing was conducted using the Illumina NovaSeq 6500 platform, achieving an average sequencing depth of 60 million reads per sample. Raw sequencing data were demultiplexed by the Illumina Dragen BioIT accelerator, followed by trimming, counting, removal of PCR duplicates, and alignment to the human reference genome hg19 using the STAR aligner (RRID:SCR_016294). Expression levels were quantified as Transcripts Per Million Molecules (TPM) through the Salmon expression pipeline. Genes associated with fatty acid metabolism and the redox pathway were log2(TPM+1) transformed and subsequently z-scored. The mean z-score of all genes within a specific pathway was then compared across different study cohorts.
Statistics
Chi-square, Fisher’s Exact, Mann-Whitney U and t-tests (with Wech’s correction) were used and adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method where appropriate. Statistical significance was considered when q<0.05.
Ethics Statement (Clinical data)
This retrospective study was conducted under Caris Life Sciences’ Research Data Banking protocol, which was reviewed and granted IRB exemption by the WCG (Western-Copernicus Group) IRB. The study adhered to the ethical guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki, the Belmont Report, and the U.S. Common Rule
Pharmacological inhibitors
CVT-11127(S4470), Erastin (S7242), Ferrostatin-1 (S7243), Staurosporin (S1421), A939572 (S9607), LY2090314 (S7063), IKE (S8877) was purchased from Selleckchem. (see also Supplementary Table S2)
Cell lines
All NSCLC cell lines were obtained from ATCC, maintained in RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS, and incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2. The following cell lines were used in this study: NCI-H358, NCI-H292, NCI-H1993, H2228, NCI-A549, and NCI-H460. All cell lines underwent fingerprinting to confirm identity and were tested mycoplasma negative before experiments, and early passages (3–5) were used for experiments.
Isogenic A549 and H460 lines reconstituted with pInducer20-GFP (Addgene_44012), pInducer20-LKB1 (Addgene_44012 and Addgene_82320), or pInducer20- KEAP1 (Addgene_44012 and Addgene_81925) were prepared by lentiviral transduction under Neomycin selection (1000ug/mL). These lentiviral vectors were adapted from our previous study [4] (see Supplementary Table S3).
Animal studies
Animal experiments were approved by the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) and Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (ISMMS) Animal Care and Use Committee. Tumors were measured twice weekly using calipers. Tumor dimensions were taken by caliper once weekly and tumor volume was calculated using the equation V = π/6∗L∗W2 (L length; W width). Mice were euthanized when tumor volumes exceeded 10% of the average body weight, 2 cm in any dimension, consistent body weight loss greater than 10%, or severe tumor ulceration.
Nude mouse model
2×106 cells were mixed with a 1:1 mixture of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and Matrigel (#CB40234, Fisher) and were injected subcutaneously into the flanks of 6-week-old female nude mice obtained from ENVIGO (Boyertown, PA). Mice were randomized into control and treatment groups (n≥8) once the mean tumor volume reached 100–150 mm3. After that mice were randomized and treated with vehicle (5% DMSO+ 40% PEG300 + 5% Tween80 + 50% saline) or A939572 (50mg/kg in 5% DMSO +40% PEG300 + 5% Tween80 + 50% saline P.O, QDx5), IKE (40mg/kg in 5% DMSO +40% PEG300 + 5% Tween80 + 50% saline IP, every other day) and combination till 90days. Tumor regression was analyzed based on the tumor volume calculation between all four groups and compared with the vehicle group.
STK11/KEAP1 re-expression Animal Studies
Mice in the +dox groups were fed a diet of doxycycline chow three days before injecting cells and throughout the experiment. Mice in the -dox group were fed a diet of amoxicillin chow to avoid skin rash. Subcutaneous flank tumors were generated by injecting 5×106 A549 (n = 5 per group) suspended in 50% Matrigel into the right flank. Tumor dimensions were taken by caliper once weekly, and tumor volume was calculated utilizing the equation V = π/6∗L∗W2 (L length; W width).
CRISPR/Cas9 Cell Lines
Small guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting human STK11, KEAP1, or SCD1 were selected from the previous paper [4]. Guides with high targeting scores and lowest probability of off target effects were chosen [4]. Guides were already cloned into lentiGuide-Puro (RRID:Addgene_52963), sgTrack-GFP (RRID:Addgene_114012), sgTrack-mCherry (RRID:Addgene_114013), or sgTrack-BFP (product of RRID:Addgene_114011 and RRID:Addgene_25891). Cloning was performed using the protocol generated by the Zhang lab (genome-engineering.org, rev20140509): Oligo annealing and cloning into backbone vectors with single-step digestion- ligation. All commercial kits used in the study are detailed in Supplementary table S4.
Lentiviral Production
Lentiviruses were produced using co-transfection of 293T cells with lentiviral backbone constructs and packaging vectors psPAX2 and pMD2.G and using Lipofectamine™ LTX Reagent with PLUS™ Reagent (Invitrogen, 15338030). Media was replaced with BSA rich media containing DMEM, 16–18 hours post transfection, and the supernatant was collected 72 hours post- transfection. The supernatant was centrifuged and collected to avoid any cell debris, and the aliquots were stored at −80°C.
Lentiviral Transduction
Cells were plated in 10cm dishes at 106 cells/dish on day 0 and allowed to attach to the plate overnight. On day 1, media was aspirated from cell plates and replaced with 10mL of fresh RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS and 8ug/mL polybrene (Tocris, R&D systems, 7711). Lentivirus from −80°C was quick-thawed in a 37°C water bath and returned to ice. Lentivirus was added to cells in a dropwise manner in a volume determined by viral titration, and cell plates were incubated overnight at 37°C. On day 2, lentiviral media was aspirated from cell plates and replaced with fresh RPMI with 10% FBS. Cell selection began on day 3, where applicable.
Cell viability (Cell Titer Glo)
Briefly, 3000 cells were seeded in white 96 well plate (Cat# 353296, Corning USA) for the cell titer-Glo assay. Cells were allowed to grow for at least 18–24 hours and treated with the different drug of our interest. After incubation with the drugs (based up on the requirement), CTG assay was done was done using previously published protocol [4]. All commercial kits used in the study are detailed in Supplementary table S4.
Drug combination data
Briefly, 3000 cells were seeded in white 96 well plate (Cat# 353296, Corning USA) for the cell titer-Glo assay. Cells were allowed to grow for at least 18–24 hours and treated with the different drugs of our interest. Mostly, two drugs were chosen for each experiment in different combination of the concentrations. After incubation with the drugs (based up on the requirement), CTG assay was done. After that synergistic effect was determined by using synergy finder software.
BODIPY/C11 staining
In a six-well plate, 0.2 ×106cells per well were seeded and allowed to attach overnight. Cells were then treated with media containing the indicated drug dose or equivalent DMSO vehicle dose and returned to incubation at 37°C. After the indicated time, drug media was supplemented with 3μM of C11-BODIPY 581/591 Lipid Peroxidation Sensor (Invitrogen, D3861) and the assay was done using previously published protocol [4].Cells treated with RSL3 for 3 hours were used as a positive control to the gate for FITC-positive cells induced by RSL3 treatment. Vehicle-treated cells were compared to drug-treated cells with a shift in the FITC curve to the right, indicating increased lipid peroxidation.
Cell line RNAseq sample preparation
Cell pellets were prepared freshly and were sent for RNA isolation, library preparation, and RNA sequencing to GENEWIZ. RNeasy Plus Universal mini kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) was used for total RNA extraction according to manufacturer’s protocol. NEBNext Ultra II RNA Library Prep Kit (NEB, Ipswich, MA, USA) was used to prepare RNA seq. library for Illumina according to manufacturer’s protocol. Agilent TapeStation (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA, USA) was used to validate RNA samples and seq. libraries. Libraries were quantified by q-PCR (KAPA Biosystems, Wilmington, MA, USA) as well as by Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA). Libraries were loaded according to manufacturer’s protocol on Illumina HiSeq instrument (4000 or equivalent) following clustering on one flowcell lane. Using a 2x150bp paired end (PE) configuration samples were sequenced and HiSeq Control Software (HCS) was used to perform image analysis and base calling. Raw sequence data (.bclfiles) were converted into fastq files and de-multiplexed using Illumina's bcl2fastq 2.17 (RRID:SCR_015058) software allowing one mismatch for index sequence identification. Raw and processed RNA-seq files were uploaded to Gene Expression Omibus database under accession (GSE262660)
RNA-Seq alignment and quality control
A total of 36 RNA-Seq libraries from 6 cell lines (NCI-H358, NCI-H661, NCI-H460, NCI-H1993, NCI-H2122, NCI-H2228), each with 3 untreated replicate samples and 3 CVT-11127 treated samples systems are processed using the same pipeline for compatibility. Quality control has been performed using FastQC (v0.11.8) (Andrews 2010). No samples were removed due to quality issues. Trim Galore! (RRID:SCR_011847) (version 0.6.5) has been used to trim the adapter sequences with a quality threshold of 20. The human genome reference used was GRCh38.p13 and GENCODE release 36 was used as the transcriptome reference. The alignment is performed by using STAR aligner (v2.7.5b) (RRID:SCR_004463) [19]. Gene level read counts are obtained by using Salmon (v1.2.1) for all libraries [18]. All samples have passed the quality control requirements with > 50% of reads uniquely mapping (>15M uniquely mapped reads for each library) using STAR aligner.
Differential expression and functional analysis
Differential expression analysis was performed using the gene level read counts and the DESeq2 (v1.28.1) R package (RRID:SCR_015687) [20]. Genes with less than 5 reads in total across all samples are filtered as inactive genes. A gene is considered differentially expressed if the adjusted p-value is less than 0.01, and the absolute log2 fold change is greater than 0.5. The over-representation functional analysis is performed using Enrichr [21] with pathway output sorted by p-value.
Heatmaps and Box plots
We performed the between sample normalization using the variance stabilizing transformation of the DESeq2 package. The 1000 most variable genes are used to perform principal component analysis as well as calculating the Euclidean distances between each sample. Gene expression heatmaps show the z-scores of DESeq2 VST normalized gene-level read counts. The heatmaps in the RNAseq analysis figure, were generated using the R package pheatmap (v1.0.12; RRID:SCR_016418), showing the uniquely up-regulated metabolites in DKO SCD1 KO cells and a curated list of DEGs, respectively.
Boxplots in lipidomics and RNAseq analyses figures, were generated using ggplot2 (v3.4.2) (RRID:SCR_014601). Boxplots in lipidomics figure for visualize important lipid classes in NTC vs DKO cells +/− SCD1 KO with the x-axis representing the number of bonds and y-axis representing raw measurements of the lipid moieties. In RNAseq figure gene expression of SIK1 and SIK1B gene in NTC vs DKO in +/− CVT-11127 condition (10μM, 96 hours).
Kinase array
The phosphorylation profiles of kinases were performed using the human Phospho-kinase array kit (ARY003C, R&D Systems) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Briefly, 0.5×106 cells/well were seeded in 6 well plate and allowed them to grow for 18hours. Then the cells were subjected to treat with the respective drugs and the combinations of the drugs of our interest. After 96 hours of incubation the cells were trypsinized, washed with PBS twice. After discarding the complete PBS, the cells were snap frozen and stored in −80°C. For quantification, dots were analyzed on Image J software using the analyze gels, plot lane command. All dots were normalized to the negative control. All commercial kits used in the study are detailed in Supplementary table S4.
Annexin-V-FITC/PI staining
0.5 ×106 cells were plated in a six-well plate in RPMI media supplemented with 10% FBS and allowed to attach to the plate overnight. On day 2, the cells were treated with the respective drugs and incubated for the required time. When the treatment was over, cells were trypsinized from the plate and washed 2x in cold PBS, followed by 1x wash in cold Annexin V binding buffer (BioLegend, 6410914). Cells were re-suspended in 100uL of Annexin V binding buffer supplemented with 5uL of Annexin V-FITC (BioLegend, 640906) and incubated at room temperature for 10 minutes in the dark. After incubation, 10uL of Propidium Iodide was added, and after gently mixing the samples, incubated for 15 minutes in the dark. 400uL Annexin V binding buffer was supplemented to each sample before acquisition. Samples were analyzed on a FACSymphony Flow Cytometer using negative controls for gating negative and negative FITC and PI. H358 NTC and DKO cells treated with 1uM Staurosporin for 8 hours were used as a positive control to gate Annexin-V-FITC and PI positive cells. Histograms of flow cytometry results were made using the FlowJo software. All commercial kits used in the study are detailed in Supplementary table S4.
Crystal violet staining
For Crystal Violate staining the cells were plated in flat bottom 96 well plate (3000cells/well) or in a 6 well-plate (0.25×106) and allowed them to grow for at least 24 hours. Then the cells were subjected to treat with the respective drugs and the combinations of the drugs of our interest. After 72–96 hours of incubation the media was discarded using multichannel pipette and the cells were washed three times with PBS and followed by staining with the 2.5% crystal violate staining solution containing methanol. After 30 minutes of incubation, the staining solution was discarded and washed 3–5 times with the PBS and photographs were captured using a scanner. All commercial kits used in the study are detailed in Supplementary table S4.
Measuring the cellular glutathione levels
Total GSH levels in the cells before and after treatment with either CVT-11127 and erastin were determined using a Glutathione Colorimetric Detection Kit (EIAGSHC, Thermo Fisher, MA). Cell lysates were prepared with 1×106 cells, and the GSH assay was performed using protocols provided by the manufacturer. All commercial kits used in the study are detailed in Supplementary table S4.
Glutathione and Cysteine Deprivation
For Glutamine and Cysteine uptake deprivation assay, 3000 cells were seeded in white 96 well plate (Cat# 353296, Corning USA) for the cell titer-Glo assay. Cells were allowed to grow for at least 18–24 hours. After that, the cells were replaced with Cysteine/Glutamine deprived media ( MP Biomedicals™ 091646454) supplemented only with of Pen strep and 10% fetal bovine serum and reading was captured after every 24 hours for the cellular viability (till 72H). For the same crystal violate staining was also performed according to the protocol described before.
RNA extraction and Quantitative real-time PCR
RNA was extracted by TRIzol reagent (Thermo, USA) and reverse transcribed to cDNA by using High-capacity cDNA synthesis kit (Applied Bio system, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instruction. Briefly, 1X106 cells were taken for the RNA extraction and finally 1μg RNA was converted to cDNA and for further analysis. Real-time PCR was done using SYBR Select Master Mix (Life Technologies, cat# 4472908) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The primers were purchased from Sigma; the details of the primers can be found in Supplementary Table S5. Triplicate PCR reactions were run on ABI (7500 Fast Real Time PCR System) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The comparative Ct method using the average 2ΔΔCT value for each set of triplicates was used, and the average of the biological replicates was calculated. Negative controls were included for every primer set to avoid any false positive result and GAPDH was used as the positive control. All commercial kits used in the study are detailed in Supplementary table S4. and primer sequences can be found in Supplementary table S5.
Immunoblotting
Total proteins were extracted with RIPA lysis buffer (Cat# 89900). Extracted proteins were estimated by Bradford method for the western blot analysis. Western blot was performed using previously published protocol [4]. The list of the primary antibodies is in Supplementary Table S6. The bands were visualized by ECL (pierce, Thermo Fisher, USA) reagent in IBRIGHT (Thermo, USA) instrument.
siRNA-Transfection
For siRNA transfection experiments, 0.5 × 106cells were plated in a 6‐well plate and allowed to reach 75% confluency. Cells were transfected with 10nM of anti‐SCD siRNA and scrambled/control (10 nM) siRNA (AM4611, Invitrogen) using Lipofectamin 3000 reagent (L3000015, Invitrogen). After 16 h incubation at 37°C 5% CO2, the media was changed with fresh RPMI media to avoid any kind of toxicity, and the cells were collected after 48 hours of transfection for qRT-PCR and western blot analysis to validate the transfection and for further investigation
TBARS assay for Malondialdehyde (MDA) Estimation
To measure the MDA, H358 NTC and DKO and H2122 cells were plated in 10 cm dishes and allowed them to grow for 24 hours. After 24H cells were subjected to treat with 10μM of CVT-11127 SCD1i. After 96 hours of treatment the cells were trypsin zed and washed with cold PBS. For MDA measurement 1× 107 Cells were taken for each condition measured using a TBARS assay kit (Cayman: No.10009055) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. (Supplementary table S4)
Lipidomics analysis
Frozen cell pellets were thawed and extracted using a protocol as previously described (Winer et al., 2024) [22]. Briefly, cells were first resuspended in 300 μL of methanol containing SPLASH LIPIDOMIX (Avanti Polar Lipids) as internal standards, followed by vortexing and the addition of 600 μL of chloroform. To facilitate phase separation, 180 μL of water was introduced into each tube. The samples were then thoroughly mixed and centrifuged at 16,000g for 5 minutes at 4°C. The lower chloroform layer was extracted, while the aqueous phase underwent a second extraction using a solution of chloroform:methanol:water (3:48:47 v/v/v). The newly extracted chloroform layer was then combined with the initial extract. Following this, the samples were dried under a nitrogen stream at 40°C and reconstituted in 100 μL of a 90:10 methanol:chloroform mixture.
Lipid profiling was conducted using an Agilent 6546 Q-TOF mass spectrometer operated in both positive and negative ionization modes, coupled with a ZORBAX Eclipse Plus C-18 column (100 mm × 2.1 mm; 1.8-μm particle size; Agilent). The mobile phase consisted of two solutions: Mobile Phase A contained 10 mM ammonium formate in a mixture of 50:30:20 water:acetonitrile:isopropanol, while Mobile Phase B contained 10 mM ammonium formate in 1:9:90 water:acetonitrile:isopropanol. The liquid chromatography (LC) gradient was programmed as follows: 0 min at 0% B, 2.7 min at 45% B, 2.8 min at 53% B, 9 min at 65% B, 9.10 min at 89% B, 11 min at 92% B, 11.10 min at 100% B, 12 min at 10% B, and held at 10% B until 15 min. Other LC parameters included a flow rate of 0.4 mL/min, a column temperature of 60°C, and an injection volume of 5 μL.
Mass spectrometry (MS) source conditions were set as follows: gas temperature at 200°C, gas flow at 10 L/min, nebulizer pressure at 50 psi, sheath gas temperature at 300°C, sheath gas flow at 12 L/min, Vcap at 3000 V, nozzle voltage at 0 V, and fragmentor at 150 V. For lipid annotation, a pooled lipid extract was subjected to five iterative tandem MS (MS/MS) injections in both positive and negative polarity.
To identify lipid species, iterative MS/MS acquisition data in positive and negative polarity was processed using Agilent Lipid Annotator software 1.0. Subsequent targeted feature extraction and peak integration were performed using Skyline. For the analysis, raw metabolite values were log10-transformed and z-score standardized. Differential metabolites were identified using the R package Limma (v3.48.0) [23], and a metabolite was considered differential if the adjusted p-value was less than 0.05 and the absolute log2 fold change was greater than 1.5. The two comparison groups were NTC +/− SCD1 KO and DKO +/− SCD1 KO.
Survival analysis
Survival analysis was calculated using R package Survival (v3.2.11; RRID: SCR_021137) using a cox regression model to identify significance between conditions. Survival plots were made with R package Survminer (v0.4.9; RRID: SCR_021094).
Statistical analysis
For comparisons among multiple groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and between two groups, student t-test was done followed by the Bonferroni post hoc test was utilized using the Graph Pad Prism version 10 software or R ggpubr(v0.4.0; RRID:021139). The p > .05 (ns), <0.05 (*), 0.01 (**), <0.001 (***) were considered as significant. Error bar represents the ±standard error of the mean (SEM) and the results are representation of n= either 2 or 3 based up on the experiments. All the statistical data were analyzed by the statistician.
For in-vivo experiments, to estimate the association between time and tumor-volume for each treatment and time and body weight, we used linear mixed-effects regression models. These models included tumor-volume (or body weight) as the dependent variable (Y), whilst including independent variables (X) Time (days or weeks) as a continuous variable and Treatment Group (Vehicle, A939572, IKE, Combination), including interaction terms between Time and Treatment. To account for repeated measures (over time) from the same mouse, we included a random intercept and random slope across MouseID, assuming an auto-regressive (AR) covariance structure across time.
Data availability
All raw data generated in this study is available upon request from the corresponding author. Raw and processed RNA-seq files were uploaded to Gene Expression Omibus database under accession GSE262660.
The data supporting this study's findings are available from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) PanCancer Atlas of Lung Adenocarcinoma at cBioPortal. These data were derived from the following public domain resources: https://gdc.cancer.gov/about-data/publications/pancanatlas. Additional public data is available from TNMplot exploring lung tissue in normal and tumor samples. These data were derived from the following public domain resources: https://tnmplot.com/analysis/.
Results
Multi-omic characterization demonstrates higher expression of key ferroptosis evasion genes SCD1 and SLC7A11 in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant LUADs.
We collaborated with Caris to evaluate a large real-world cohort of KRASmut-LUAD specimens (n=5498) stratified by the mutation status of STK11 and KEAP1 (Fig. 1A, TCGA data S1A). Patients with KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut had a lower median age at tumor biopsy (70 vs 67 years old, q<0.0001) and the co-mutant tumors were more prevalent in males (50.9% vs 38.9%, q<0.0001) compared to tumors with KRASmut/STK11wt/KEAP1wt (Supplementary Table S1).
We observed a higher expression of ferroptosis regulators, SCD1 [17] and SLC7A11 [24], [25], in KRAS mutant LUADs and particularly in the KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut LUADs (Supplementary Table S7, S8, Fig. 1B and 1C). Next, we investigated the expression of SCD1 and SLC7A11 in an independent lung cancer clinical dataset. As expected SCD1 (p<0.001) and SLC7A11 (p<0.001) expression were appreciably higher in LUADs as compared to normal tissue (Supplementary Table S9, Fig. 1D and 1E). Interestingly, SCD1 and SLC7A11 expressions were positively correlated in KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut LUADs (Fig. 1F, r=0.35, p<0.001). The correlation of SCD1 and SLC7A11, the two master regulators of ferroptosis evasion, underscores the upregulation of ferroptosis protection programs in KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut LUADs. Analysis of top upregulated pathways demonstrated that redox pathway and fatty acid metabolism were enriched in tumors with concomitant mutations in KRAS, STK11, and KEAP1 as compared to single mutants or wild type counterparts (Fig 1G and 1H, p<0.001).
In the Caris dataset, higher expression of SCD1 and SLC7A11 was associated with worse overall survival in patients with KRASmut-LUAD (Fig. 1I and 1J). KRASmut-LUAD patients with high SCD1 expression had a median OS of 17.66 months (mo) compared to 24.21mo in patients with SCD1 low expression (Fig. 1I; p<0.001, HR=1.221). Moreover, KRASmut-LUAD patients with high SLC7A11 expression had a median OS of 14.67mo compared to 27.96mo in patients with low SLC7A11 expression (Fig. 1J; p<0.001, HR=1.53). Similarly, high SCD1 and SLC7A11 expressions predicted worse outcomes in patients in the TCGA LUAD dataset (Fig. S1B and S1C; p<0.05).
Taken together, the data demonstrates that genetically defined subsets of KRASmut-LUADs with concurrent loss of STK11 and KEAP1 have comparatively higher expression of key ferroptosis evasion genes, SCD1 and SLC7A11. The expression of these key metabolic regulators was correlated and high expression of SCD1 and SLC7A11 predicted poor prognosis in KRASmut LUADs.
Targeting SCD1 decreases the viability and augments the cytotoxic effect of SLC7A11 inhibition in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant LUAD models.
To investigate the mechanism of action by which SCD1 and SLC7A11 drive ferroptosis evasion in KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut LUAD models, we examined a library of LUAD cell lines with de novo KRAS wild type (H292), KRAS mutation (H358), concurrent de novo mutation of KRAS/STK11 (H1993), concurrent de novo mutation of KRAS/KEAP1 (H2228), and KRAS mutant cell lines with concurrent de novo loss of STK11/KEAP1 (H2122, H460, A549), along with an EGFR mutant (H827) and TP53 mutant cell lines (H827 and H1975). In agreement with the gene expression data, both SCD1 and SLC7A11 protein expression was appreciably higher in KRAS mutant cell lines with concurrent de novo loss of STK11/KEAP1 (Fig. S1D, S1E, S1F) compared to wild type or single mutant models.
Next, we employed CRISPR Cas9 to create stable knockouts (KO) of STK11, KEAP1, or both genes (double knockout: DKO) in H358 cells (KRAS mutation: G12C) (Fig. S1G). Interestingly, western blot analysis demonstrated a substantial increase in the expression of SCD1 and SLC7A11 after STK11 and KEAP1 knockout (Fig. S1H), compared to single gene knockout or wild-type models. In agreement with the protein data, RNA sequencing of the models demonstrated that the mRNA expression of SLC7A11 was higher in the KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co- mutant model compared to double mutants or wild type (Fig. S1I). We also correlated the expression of broader set of ferroptosis-related genes (Fig. S1J) to SCD1 or SLC7A11 in our clinical data set. A number of genes including AKR1C1, AKR1C2, CYP4F11, AKR1B10, GPX2, G6PD, GCLM and GCLC were enriched in KRASMUT/STK11MUT/KEAP1MUT & KRASMUT/STK11WT/KEAP1MUT compared to KRASMUT/STK11WT/KEAP1WT–LUAD (Fig. S1J). This demonstrates that concurrent KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 mutation is associated with an increase in the expression of ferroptosis evasion genes, primarily, SCD1 and SLC7A11 (Fig S1E, S1F) which potentially promotes survival of the KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant preclinical models.
In H358 cells (KRASmut/STK11wt/KEAP1wt), treatment with a ferroptosis inhibitor, ferrostatin-1 (fer-1), led to a notable time-dependent increase in proliferation compared to non-treated control (Fig. 2A). This highlights the role of ferroptosis as a barrier to cell proliferation and growth in a LUAD model with wild type STK11 and KEAP1. Next, we treated a panel of KRASmut-LUAD cells (H292, H358, H1993, H2228, and H2122) differing in STK11 and KEAP1 mutation status (described above) with erastin, which inhibits xCT-mediated cysteine transport. Accumulating evidence has indicated that suppression of cysteine (a rate-limiting biosynthetic precursor of GSH) uptake by SLC7A11 inhibitor, erastin, results in the accumulation of lipid peroxides, eventually triggering ferroptosis [12], [26]. Higher IC50 concentrations of erastin in H2122 (KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut) compared to other KRASmut-LUAD cells, suggest a higher inherent resistance to erastin-induced ferroptosis in this genotype (Fig. 2B). Similar results were observed in the H358 isogenic cell lines, wherein erastin treatment appreciably inhibited the viability of LUAD cells with STK11wt and KEAP1wt (Fig. 2B). However, cells with concurrent loss of STK11 and KEAP1 (de novo or stable knockout) were appreciably more resistant to erastin treatment (Fig. 2C). Consistent with induction of ferroptosis via distinct mechanisms, co-inhibition of SCD1 (CVT-11127) and SLC7A11 (erastin) resulted in a synergistic decrease in cell viability in H2122 (KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut) compared to H358 (KRASmut/STK11wt/KEAP1wt) cells (Fig. 2D and 2E). Crystal violet staining confirmed the growth inhibitory effect of dual SCD1 and SLC7A11 inhibition in the isogenic DKO compared to NTC cells (Fig. S2A, S2B, and S2C). Fer-1 treatment successfully abrogated the cytotoxic effect of CVT-11127 (SCD1 inhibitor) treatment with or without erastin in DKO cells (Fig. S2A, S2B, and S2C). Moreover, CVT-11127 treatment did not induce apoptosis in DKO cells (Fig. S2D). This suggests that CVT-11127 treatment does not cause an appreciable decrease in cell viability in STK11wt/KEAP1wt models, causes cell death in STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant models through ferroptosis, and meaningfully enhances the efficacy of ferroptosis inducer, erastin.
We hypothesized that enhanced intracellular reactive oxygen species levels upon SCD1 inhibition were likely due to the induction of lipid peroxidation [27]. Pharmacological inhibition of SCD1 alone produced appreciably more lipid peroxidation (analyzed by C11-BODIPY staining) in KRAS mutant models with de novo loss of STK11 and KEAP1 (H2122) as compared to wild type STK11 and KEAP1 cell line (H358) (Fig. 2F and 2G). Likewise, pharmacological inhibition of SLC7A11 (erastin treatment) led to increased ferroptosis in H358 (KRASmut/STK11wt/KEAP1wt) compared to H2122 (KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut) cells. This further confirms that KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant models have resistance to ferroptosis induction due to higher expression of ferroptosis evasion genes. However, dual inhibition of SCD1 and SLC7A11 causes comparatively higher lipid peroxidation in H2122 than in H358, which shows SCD1/SLC7A11 axis as a vulnerability in KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut LUAD models. Co-treatment with Fer-1 could prevent cells from producing excessive lipid peroxidation (Fig. 2F and 2G). To measure lipid peroxidation, we next performed the TBARS assay for malondialdehyde (MDA) estimation in the wildtype and co-mutant models. We demonstrate that pharmacological inhibition of SCD1 (with CVT-11127) upregulated lipid peroxides in the isogenic H358 DKO and H2122 de novo co-mutant models, compared to H358 NTC (Fig 2H).
Together, the findings demonstrated that KRAS mutant tumors with co-occurring loss of STK11 and KEAP1 have consequential enrichment of redox and fatty acid metabolism pathways. Moreover, SCD1 and SLC7A11 inhibition led to an increase in lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis, and decreased viability of KRAS mutant cells with concurrent loss of STK11 and KEAP1.
SCD1 inhibition increases cystine uptake by xCT and promotes GSH synthesis in the KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut LUAD model.
Most cancer cells mainly rely on SLC7A11 to mediate the uptake of extracellular cystine in exchange for glutamate [28]. Therefore, next we investigated the effect of SCD1 targeting on the cellular GSH levels in the H358 NTC and DKO cells. As expected, we observed an appreciable decrease in GSH levels in DKO cells compared to the NTC after pharmacological inhibition of SCD1 (Fig. 2I, 2J). Combined inhibition of SLC7A11 (erastin) and SCD1 (CVT-11127) led to an appreciable decrease in GSH levels (Fig. 2I, 2J). Insufficient GSH production suggests an appreciable imbalance in the cellular redox system, which leads to metabolic rewiring in the DKO cells.
As xCT is an antiporter that exchanges intracellular glutamate for extracellular cystine and is the sole importer of cystine, we further examined whether SCD1 inhibition leads to differential resistance to cystine deprivation. Since we observed differential sensitivity to SCD1 inhibitor and erastin in cells in H358 NTC and DKO cells, we next investigated the differences between these models to cystine deprivation by time-dependent dilution of cystine in the medium (24, 48, and 72H). Interestingly, we observed an appreciable decrease in cell survival only in the NTC cells but not in the DKO or H2122 or A549 cells (de novo KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut) (Fig. 2K, 2L, S2E). Moreover, complete cystine depletion from the media did not appreciably affect the survival of the DKO cells, whereas NTC cells exhibited appreciably higher cell death, demonstrating notable resilience to cystine deprivation in cells with STK11/KEAP1 co-mutation (Fig. 2K, 2L, S2E).
Taking together, we demonstrate that the DKO cells maintain more cystine due to the overexpression of SLC7A11, which protects the cells from external oxidative pressures. In contrast, SCD1 inhibition leads to metabolic rewiring in the DKO cells, further disrupting the cellular redox balance by depleting the GSH levels and increasing ferroptotic sensitivity in the cells.
Targeting SCD1 upregulates free fatty acid in the KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant lung cancer cells, leading to lipid peroxidation-mediated cell death.
SCD1 is a critical component of metabolism, hence, next, we performed liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis in H358 NTC and DKO models with or without CRISPR-mediated knockdown of SCD1 to define the lipidome of these cells. SCD1 depletion impacted H358 NTC and DKO cells differentially, resulting in 18 lipid species upregulated in H358 NTC cells (Fig. 3A), and 90 lipid species upregulated in H358 DKO cells (Fig. 3B), of which 87 were uniquely upregulated in DKO cells (Fig. 3C, 3D). Upregulated lipid classes included phosphatidylinositol (PI), ether-linked phosphatidylethanolamine (EtherPE), lysophosphatidylglycerol (LPG) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) (Fig 3E, F, G, H). Furthermore, detailed analysis of the fatty acid profile revealed that SCD1 depletion led to the upregulation of PUFAs with two or more double bonds in H358 DKO cells (Fig 3E, F, G, H). Accumulation of lipid species with unstable and highly reactive multiple double bonds provided evidence for lipid peroxidation as the underlying mechanism of ferroptosis in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant cells (Fig. 3I).
Pharmacological inhibition of SCD1 leads to suppression of salt-inducible kinase genes (SIK1, SIK1B) in KRASmut-LUAD models with concomitant loss of STK11 and KEAP1.
We next performed bulk RNA sequencing of cells with de novo loss of STK11, KEAP1, or both genes pre- and post- CVT-11127 (SCD1 inhibitor) treatment. We identified 109 genes that were exclusively downregulated in KRAS mutant cells with de novo loss of STK11 and KEAP1 post- CVT-11127 treatment (p<0.05) (Fig. 4A). Analysis of the 109 downregulated genes in STK11/KEAP1 co- mutant model highlighted glutathione and glutamic acid as the top downregulated pathways post SCD1 inhibition (Fig. 4B). As expected, the top genes suppressed in STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant model post-CVT-11127 treatment included genes involved in ferroptosis (SELENOP, GSTA1, GGT6), redox (VNN1, TXNIP), fatty acid metabolism (SOAT1, SPNS2, PPARGC1A), other crucial pathways, such as glutathione and glutamic acid pathways (Fig. 4C). Interestingly, two of the genes uniquely downregulated in H2122 (KRAS mutant cell with de novo loss of STK11/KEAP1) were salt-inducible kinase genes (SIK1, SIK1B) that belong to the AMPK family and play an important role in gluconeogenesis and lipid metabolism [29]. Previous studies have shown that SIK1 represses lipogenic gene expression, such as Scd1, possibly via an SREBPs-mediated transcriptional regulation in a hepatic lipogenesis model [29,30]. Studies have shown conflicting roles of SIKs as a tumor suppressor or an oncogene in LUAD and pancreatic cancer [31], [32], [33].
Interestingly, using the isogenic cell lines, we observed that SIK1 and SIK1B were upregulated post-CVT-11127 treatment in H358 (KRASmut) and downregulated in H2122 (KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut) potentially highlighting genotype-specific associations (Fig. 4D, E). When comparing H358 and H2122 cells, we observed a downregulation of SIK1 and related genes (CREB, and SCD1) post-CVT-11127 treatment exclusively in H2122 (KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut) cells (Fig. 4F and 4G). It is noteworthy that the H358 DKO model had an appreciably higher baseline expression of SIK1 as compared to H358 NTC (Fig. 4H). We next investigated the time dependent effect SCD1 inhibition on SIK1 expression. We treated H358 NTC and H358 DKO with CVT-11127 for 24, 48, 72 and 96 hours. We found that SCD1 inhibition led to downregulation of SIK1 expression in H358 DKO cells and the de novo triple mutant H2122 cells (Fig 4I). Whereas SCD1 inhibition led to time-dependent increase in SIK1expression in H358 NTC cells (Fig 4I), confirming our RNAseq finding. Furthermore, we observed a weaker correlation in KRASmut/STK11wt/KEAP1wt (Fig. S2F: r=0.12, p<0.0001) and a stronger positive correlation between SCD1 and SIK1 in the KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut (Fig. S2G: r=0.29, p<0.0001) tumor samples.
In summary, we show that SCD1 inhibition causes unique transcriptomic changes in LUAD cells which is dependent on the mutation status of STK11 and KEAP1. SCD1 inhibition leads to consequential downregulation of glutathione and glutamic acid pathways (p<0.005) highlighting the potential role of SCD1 in survival and glutathione-mediated ferroptosis in co-mutant cells. Finally, pharmacological inhibition of SCD1 leads to suppression of salt-induced kinases, SIK1 and SIK1B in a genotype specific manner.
Targeting SCD1 uniquely modulates AKT/GSK3β/NRF2 pathway in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant model.
We explored SCD1-mediated changes in downstream signaling by targeted kinase profiling. The effect of SCD1 inhibition (by CVT-11127) on 37 major oncogenic kinases was measured by a targeted kinase array in H358 NTC and DKO cells (Fig. 5A). We observed differential modulation of 17 oncogenic kinases between NTC and DKO models post-SCD1 targeting (Fig. S3A). 8/17 differentially modulated oncogenic kinases were further analyzed based on their reported roles in cancer cell metabolism, proliferation, and survival (Fig. 5B). GSK3β S9, PLCγ1, β-catenin, STAT3, WNK1, HSP60, ERK1/2, and CHK2 were differentially regulated in NTC and DKO after treatment with CVT-11127 (Fig. 5B).
We next demonstrated that not only SCD1 expression is positively correlated with SLC7A11 expression in KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut models (Fig. 1F), pharmacological inhibition of SCD1 (CVT-11127 at 10μM, 96 hours), decreases the expression of SLC7A11 (about 70%) in KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut model (Fig. 5C, S3B). SCD1 is known to regulate the AKT-GSK3β axis in multiple cancer types [17]. However, the role of SCD1 inhibition in regulating the AKT-GSK3β pathway in the context of STK11/KEAP1 mutations in LUAD models is unknown. Pharmacological inhibition of SCD1 (CVT-11127 at 10μM, 96 hours) led to a decrease in pAKT-S473 (about 90%) and a decrease in pS21/9-GSK3β (about 35%) (inhibitory phosphorylation) exclusively in DKO cells. A decrease in inhibitory phosphorylation of GSK3β (about 35%) indicates the activation of GSK3β in DKO cells (Fig. 5C, S3B). As evidenced in the control group in DKO, high baseline SCD1 expression is associated with higher phosphorylated AKT and pS21/9-GSK3β resulting in inactive GSK3 signaling (Fig. 5C, S3B). To confirm whether the changes observed were due to off-target effects of CVT-11127 treatment, we performed siRNA-mediated knockdown of SCD1 in DKO model (Fig. 5D, S3C, S3D). In agreement with pharmacological inhibition, genetic inhibition of SCD1 also decreased the expression of SLC7A11(about 86%) (Fig. 5D, S3D). Moreover, SCD1 inhibition also increased the expression of the iron receptor, transferrin receptor (TFRC); while suppressing major iron transporters such as SLC11A2 (DMT1), ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1); and master regulator of ferroptosis GPX4 (Fig. 5D, S3D).
AKT upregulates the SLC7A11 and NRF2 expression with co-occurring depletion of GSK3β in different cancer types and physiological conditions [34], [35]. Similarly, In DKO cells, if SCD1 inhibition promoted ferroptosis by GSK3β activation, we hypothesized that inhibiting GSK3β would overcome SCD1-mediated ferroptosis in these cells. To investigate this role of GSK3β, we treated H358 NTC and DKO cells with GSK3β inhibitor LY2090314 (30nM, 24H) or SCD1 inhibitor, CVT-11127 (10μM, 96 hours). In NTC cells, CVT-11127 treatment did not change the expression of pS21/9-GSK3β or SLC7A11, however, LY2090314 treatment led to a decrease in SLC7A11 expression (Fig. 5E, S3E). In DKO cells CVT-11127 treatment decreased the expression of pS21/9-GSK3β (and total GSK3β levels) as well as SLC7A11, while LY2090314 treatment led to an increase in NRF2 and SLC7A11 expression (Fig. 5E, S3E). This demonstrated the effect of GSK3β on NRF2 and SLC7A11 expression in DKO model. We next investigated the time dependent effect of SCD1 inhibition on the protein expression of key signaling changes (like SIK1, SLC7A11, and GSK3B). CVT-11127 treatment for 24, 48, 72 and 96 hours led to the time-dependent downregulation of SIK1, SLC7A11 and pGSK3β Ser21/9 (inhibitory phosphorylation site) expression in H358 DKO cells and the de novo triple mutant H2122 (Fig 5F, S3F, S3G), but not in H358 NTC cells (Fig 5F, S3F).
Furthermore, LY2090314 treatment was able to rescue CVT-11127 treatment-mediated ferroptosis induction in DKO cells (Fig. 5G). Conversely, given the lack of induction of lipid peroxidation by CVT-11127 treatment in NTC cells, co-treatment with LY2090314 did not further influence lipid peroxidation (Fig. 5G). Crystal violet staining demonstrated agreement with the lipid peroxidation data (Fig. 5H) supporting the involvement of GSK3β in SCD1-mediated ferroptosis in KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut cells.
In summary, our data shows that SCD1 targeting uniquely modulates the AKT/GSK3β pathway in LUAD with dual STK11/KEAP1 loss. In KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut models SCD1 targeting activates GSK3β leading to the downregulation of NRF2. Moreover, in agreement with previous reports, SCD1 targeting mediated NRF2 downregulation leads to suppression of SLC7A11 in the KRASmut/STK11mut/KEAP1mut model, thus, making the cells more vulnerable to ferroptosis- induced cell death.
SCD1 inhibition selectively decreases tumor growth and augments the anti- tumor response of SLC7A11 inhibition in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 in vivo.
Based on the in vitro potency of SCD1 inhibition alone or when combined with SLC7A11 inhibition, we next investigated the anti-tumor effect of A939572 and IKE in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant in vivo model. Mice were injected with H358- NTC and DKO cells (with STK11/KEAP1 knockout). When tumors reached a volume of 100–150 mm3, the mice from each model were randomized into four treatment groups: i) Vehicle, (ii) SCD1 inhibitor A939572 (50mg/kg, 5/7 days), (iii) SLC7A11 inhibitor, Imidazole ketone erastin (IKE) (40mg/kg, 5/7 days) and (iv) A939572+ IKE combination (Fig. 6A).
As expected, in the H358 NTC model, single-agent IKE treatment caused a delay in tumor growth (Fig. 6 B, C, D, E, F). However, single agent A939572 treatment did not cause any tumor regression in the H358 NTC model (Fig. 6 B, C, D, E, F). In the NTC model, the combined inhibition of SCD1 and SLC7A11 showed a similar antitumor effect as SLC7A11 (IKE treatment) alone, showing that the combination treatment did not have any additional anti-tumor effect (Fig. 6B–F). We did not observe notable toxicity of the single agent or the combination treatment of the drugs as evident by no appreciable changes in SCR and ALT levels in the liver function test (Fig. 6G, H).
However, in the H358 DKO model, as expected, the single-agent IKE treatment did not cause any remarkable delay in tumor growth (Fig. 6I). In contrast, the single agent A939572 treatment group showed an appreciable delay in tumor growth (p=0.001; decrease by ~58.5%), (Fig. 6I). This further confirms that SCD1 plays an essential role in DKO models as compared to the NTC model. Finally, the combined treatment of A939572 and IKE caused an appreciable tumor regression, with a ~74.4% decrease in tumor volume compared to the vehicle group at day 65 (p<0.001) (Fig. 6I, J, K, L, M). At day 65 tumor of the vehicle group was 1210 mm3, whereas co-treatment group had 310 mm3 (74.4% tumor volume reduction). Moreover, in the combination group, the tumor volume of 7 out of 10 mice was below baseline tumor volume at day 75. At day 90, 8 out of 10 mice in the combination group had tumor volume below baseline tumor volume (Fig. 6 J, K, L, M) (p<0.001). SCD1 inhibition in combination with SLC7A11 inhibition caused appreciably more tumor regression in the DKO model than SCD1 inhibition alone. As expected, the combined inhibition of SCD1 and SLC7A11 led to considerable survival benefit (S4A, S4B). Similarly, we did not observe any toxicity of the drugs as a single agent or the combination in the H358 DKO xenograft model as shown by no appreciable change in the liver function data (Fig. 6N, 6O).
We collected the endpoint tumors to assess the effect of SCD1 inhibition of key ferroptosis markers. Notably, in H358 DKO tumors (and not in H358 NTC tumors), treatment with SCD1 inhibitor (A939572) leads to decreased mRNA expression of SLC7A11 and GPX4, the two master regulators of ferroptosis (Fig S4C). Hence A939572-mediated decrease in SLC7A11 and GPX4 expression demonstrates ferroptosis induction in KRASmutSTK11mutKEAP1mut model.
We next validated our findings in two additional cell line xenograft models (A549 and H460) harboring de novo KRAS, STK11, and KEAP1 co-mutations to confirm the anti-tumor response of SCD1 inhibitor with or without SLC7A11 inhibition. We transduced A549 cells, both with doxycycline-inducible lentiviral vectors expressing either STK11wt (LKB1) or KEAP1wt [4]. As previously shown, A549 cells demonstrated tightly regulated, doxycycline-inducible expression of LKB1 or KEAP1 protein and a decrease in NRF2 upon re-expression of KEAP1 [4]. A549 control cells (GFP+DOX), A549 cells with LKB1 re-expression (LKB1+DOX), or with KEAP1 re-expression (KEAP1+DOX) were injected subcutaneously into the flanks of 4–5 weeks old female athymic nude mice. When tumors reached a volume of 100–150 mm3, the mice from each model were randomized into four treatment groups: i) Vehicle, (ii) SCD1 inhibitor A939572, appropriate for in vivo study (50mg/kg, 5/7 days), (iii) SLC7A11 inhibitor, Imidazole ketone erastin (IKE), appropriate for in vivo study (40mg/kg, 5/7 days) and (iv) A939572+ IKE combination (Fig. 6A).
Confirming our in vitro findings, single-agent IKE treatment did not cause tumor regression in A549 control tumors (~14.8% at Day 50), while single-agent A939572 treatment led to a modest delay in tumor growth (~51% at Day 50) (Fig. 7A). However, we observed notable tumor regression upon co-treatment with A939572+ IKE which was more than either of the single agents (Fig. 7A). At day 50 tumor of the vehicle group was 1310 mm3, whereas co-treatment group had 262mm3 (~80% reduction at Day 50) (p<0.001). Moreover, the combination treatment also improved survival in this model (Fig S4D).
Interestingly, re-expression of LKB1 in A549 models sensitized tumors to single agent IKE as compared to parental A549 (~36.3% decrease by day 60) (Fig. 7B). On the other hand, the tumors with re-expression of LKB1 were relatively more resistant to single-agent SCD1 inhibition as compared to parental A549 (~16% decrease by day 60) (Fig. 7B). Finally, re-expression of LKB1 appeared to rescue the anti-tumor response of combined inhibition of SCD1 and SLC7A11 and no appreciable tumor regression was observed after adding back the LKB1 in the system (Fig. 7B).
In A549 cells with add back of KEAP1 (KEAP1+DOX), a very distinct tumor profile was observed (Fig. 7C). First, the overall tumor growth rate of the vehicle group was comparatively slower than control groups of A549 parental or A549 with LKB1 re-expressed (Fig. 7C). As with LKB1 re- expressed tumors, KEAP1 re-expression also led to relative resistance to SCD1 inhibition (Fig. 7C). Whereas the models were relatively more sensitive to single agent IKE and modest delay in tumor growth was observed (Fig. 7C). Finally, re-expression of KEAP1 also reversed the anti- tumor response of combined A939572 and IKE treatment and no appreciable tumor regression was observed after adding back the KEAP1 in the system (Fig. 7C).
We next investigated the effect of SCD1 inhibition (A939572) with or without ferroptosis inducer (IKE) in an additional de novo triple mutant cell line xenograft model (H460). As expected, the single-agent IKE treatment did not cause any pronounced delay in tumor growth (only 7.5% at day 55) (Fig. 7D). In contrast, the single-agent A939572 treatment group showed a delay in tumor growth (p=0.001; tumor regression of ~36% at day 55) (Fig. 7D). Finally, the combined treatment of A939572 and IKE caused notable tumor regression, with a ~58% decrease in tumor volume compared to the vehicle group at day 55 (p<0.001) (Fig. 7D). The combination treatment also improved survival in the H460 when compared to the vehicle or single agent treatment groups (Fig. S4E). Finally, the treatment did not cause any toxicity (Fig 7E, F) or notable changes in body weight (Fig. 7G), which underscores the safety of the treatment regimens (Fig. 7E–G, S4E).
Our data shows that LUAD models with STK11/KEAP1 co-mutation are relatively more resistant to the ferroptosis inducer, and IKE treatment, and relatively more sensitive to single-agent SCD1 inhibition. Moreover, SCD1 inhibition appreciably augments the anti-tumor and survival benefit of ferroptosis inducer, IKE, in models with a combined loss of STK11 and KEAP1. Re-expression of STK11 or KEAP1 overcomes the anti-tumor benefit of SCD1 and SLC7A11 combined inhibition. This highlights that SCD1 inhibition with or without ferroptosis inducer is an effective therapeutic strategy in STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant LUAD.
Discussion
Advanced LUADs with loss-of-function mutations in STK11 and KEAP1 are remarkably aggressive and unresponsive to chemotherapy and immunotherapy, the current care standards [36], [37], [38], [39]. Despite STK11/KEAP1 being two of the most frequently co-mutated genes in human LUAD and a well-established predictor of worse outcomes, the mechanisms by which these co-mutations drive tumorigenesis is still not well understood. Herein, we present a transcriptomic analysis of a real-world cohort of about 5500 KRAS mutant LUAD tumors. We demonstrate that KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutants have appreciably high expression of fatty acid metabolism, redox pathway, and master regulators of ferroptosis, SCD1, and SLC7A11. In this study, we show that SCD1 and SLC7A11 expression is positively correlated in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant LUADs. Second, SCD1 directly regulates the expression and function of SLC7A11 through the AKT-GSK3β-β-NRF2 axis. Third, SCD1 inhibition regulates cystine import, generation of GSH, and PUFAs synthesis promoting ferroptotic death. Fourth, SCD1 inhibition in combination with ferroptosis inducer causes a notable anti- tumor effect in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant in vivo models.
Concomitant KRAS/KEAP1 alterations exhibited increased dependence on glutaminolysis and shorter survival on chemotherapy or immunotherapy [39]. Though the roles of STK11 or KEAP1 mutations have individually been studied, the biological mechanisms favoring coordinated LOF of STK11 and KEAP1 have not been fully defined. We have previously shown that ferroptosis evasion may be a key mechanism facilitating the survival and persistence of STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant NSCLC cells. However, the molecular mechanism of how the STK11/KEAP1 co-mutations influence ferroptosis in LUAD cells was not defined and has been addressed in this study. Here we demonstrate, in both patient samples and cell lines, a meaningfully positive linkage between SCD1 and SLC7A11 in STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant LUADs, which gives the LUAD cells a unique biology to evade ferroptosis and provides poor clinical outcomes in patients. In agreement with the high concurrent expression of SCD1 and SLC7A11, STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant models were resistant to ferroptosis induction as compared to wildtype models. Moreover, we demonstrate a consequential increase in the redox signaling and fatty acid metabolism pathways in a cohort of 5498 patients with KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant LUAD.
Interestingly, our data shows that salt-inducible kinases, or SIKs, were uniquely downregulated by SCD1 inhibition in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant LUAD. SIKs are AMPK family kinases mainly involved in regulating energy response-related physiological processes, such as gluconeogenesis and lipid metabolism [40]. Previous studies have shown conflicting roles of SIKs in cancer. Data show that in a LKB1-deficient model, SIK inhibition abrogates tumor growth [41], [31]. On the other hand, upregulated SIK3 enhances cell cycle progression by releasing G1/S arrest, thereby bestowing growth advantages to breast cancers [42]. These cell cycle arresting and apoptosis promotion effects were achieved by the interactions between SIK and AKT signaling pathway [43]. SIKs restrain the lipogenesis of cancer cells by governing SREBP-1 and regulate the phosphorylation of cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) and its downstream CREB-regulated transcription coactivators [40], [44]. SCD1 inhibition further downregulated the expression of the genes involved in the AMPK-SIK pathway. Therefore, our study is the first to show that, in the context of KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant LUAD, SCD1 targeting abrogates cancer growth and facilitates ferroptosis through the downregulation of SIKs, possibly through the AKT signaling pathway.
Our findings show that SCD1 inhibition, exclusively in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant models, can modulate sensitivity to ferroptosis by modulating the regulation of AKT and its substrate GSK3β. This shows the role of SCD1 on the GSK3β-NRF2 axis, which is a known modulator of ferroptosis induction. Previous work has shown that GSK3β negatively regulates fatty acid metabolism by targeting the SREBP1 and its target genes [45]. Moreover, the transcription factor NRF2, when phosphorylated by GSK3β, is degraded by β-TrCP leading to reduced tumor growth [46]. More recently, it was established that GSK3β/NRF2 signaling pathway modulated erastin- induced ferroptosis in breast cancer [47]. Here we established that SCD1 regulates SLC7A11 expression, cystine and GSH dependency, and ferroptosis-mediated cell death uniquely in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant models. We further showed that this regulation occurs via the AKT/GSK3β/NRF2 pathway. Treatment with a GSK3β inhibitor prevented AKT inhibitor-mediated ferroptosis. Moreover, GSK3β inhibition was able to reverse erastin-induced ferroptosis. Therefore, our study shows that SCD1 regulates NRF2, and SLC7A11 expression and, subsequently, promotes ferroptosis and this is primarily mediated by inhibiting AKT activity and activating GSK3β, uniquely in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant models.
KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant cells had decreased GSH levels compared to wild- type cells after SCD1 inhibition. Co-treatment of cells with SLC7A11 inhibitor (erastin) and SCD1 inhibitor (CVT-11127), led to a consistent drop in GSH levels. A previous study has shown that activating NRF2 in mammalian cancer cells leads to better dependency on exogenous glutathione through xCT [48]. In KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 cells, SCD1 inhibition downregulated glutathione metabolism and glutamic acid pathways. Decreased NRF2/SLC7A11 expression restricts glutamate availability for the TCA cycle or less cystine level impacts GSH production, creating a metabolic bottleneck in STK11/KEAP1 DKO cells. NRF2/SLC7A11 axis is high in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant cells, and SCD1 inhibition regulates the axis and promotes ferroptotic cell death.
By maintaining the lipogenesis of cancer cells, SCD1 plays a crucial role in tumor formation, progression, invasion, and metastasis [49], [50], [51], [17]. Several reports have argued that ferroptosis sensitivity is not dictated by any one specific lipid species but rather by the overall abundance of PUFAs-containing versus MUFAs-containing phospholipids [52]. Many different lipids and metabolic enzymes can contribute to ferroptosis in a context-dependent manner [53], [54], [55]. Hence, we next wanted to investigate the effect of SCD inhibition on the global lipidomic landscape in LUADs. We found that loss of SCD1 expression increases the levels of SFAs and PUFAs lipid species that are linked to the induction of ferroptosis specifically for the KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 cells. Interestingly, SFAs and PUFAs are known to cause ferroptosis in cancer cells whereas MUFAs provide protection [56], [57]. FADS2 increases the PUFAs levels after SCD1 inhibition potentially made the KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant models more susceptible to ferroptosis [58],[59],[60]. SCD1 plays a promising role in several metabolic processes, including glycolysis and lipid metabolism, which makes targeting SCD1 very advantageous for cancer therapy [58], [17]. How SCD1 expression alters membrane phospholipid composition uniquely in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 models will require further elucidation but could involve interaction with enzymes that generate lipid signaling or modulation of lipid trafficking.
Crucially, we have established the potential for combination treatments with SCD1 inhibition and SLC7A11 inhibition in multiple in vivo models of LUAD. As expected, KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant models were relatively resistant to SLC7A11 inhibition and sensitive to SCD1 inhibition. This resistance to ferroptosis was reversed with the re-expression of LKB1 and KEAP1. Erastin had a statistically significant effect on H358 KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant, H460 and A549 models when combined with SCD1 inhibition. This concordance across multiple in vitro and in vivo models increases the translational potential of this combination in patients with LUAD having KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 mutation. We anticipate and encourage others to explore this combination and utilize our dataset to uncover potential therapeutically actionable approaches for this deadly disease.
In summary, our data collectively demonstrates that SCD1 and SLC7A11 are highly expressed and correlates with worse prognosis in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant LUAD. SCD1 regulates the expression and function of a master ferroptosis regulator, SLC7A11, through the AKT-GSK3β-NRF2 pathway. We demonstrate that SCD1 inhibition-induced ferroptosis in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 mutant LUADs is associated with the accumulation of SFAs and PUFAs through the downregulation of the NRF2/SLC7A11 axis. Finally, the combined inhibition of SCD1 and SLC7A11 causes anti- tumor effect in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant in vivo models. Therefore, our study provides a framework for the combined use of preclinical models and clinical samples to investigate the impact of molecular diversity on metabolic heterogeneity, to identify clinically relevant therapeutic vulnerabilities. This study improves our understanding of ferroptosis in LUADs and our ability to target SCD1 or ferroptosis in lung cancer treatment. We provide proof-of-concept evidence that SCD1 and SLC7A11 may be relevant therapeutic targets for a genetically defined subset of LUADs with particularly poor prognosis. These agents are safe to use with acceptable toxicity and established doses, including inhibitors of SLC7A11 (Erastin/IKE), supporting further investigation of this pathway in the clinic.
Limitations of the study
As the expression of several other genes related to SCD1 are similarly upregulated in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 mutant LUADs, deep mechanistic work deconvoluting how SCD1 regulatory genes influence lipid composition of LUADs will be an important goal of future studies. Ferroptosis evasion genes play an important role in drug resistance. Therefore, additional validation in preclinical models and clinical samples from pre- and post-chemotherapy or immunotherapy treated samples is warranted to confirm the role of ferroptosis evasion genes (SCD1 and SLC7A11) in treatment resistance in KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 co-mutant LUADs. While our data demonstrates the anti-tumor response of SCD1 inhibition alone or in combination of SLC7A11 inhibition in multiple LUAD cell line xenografts, additional experiments need to be performed in orthotopic models and PDXs to validate the long-term effect and the key signaling changes of the combination treatment. Considering the role of ferroptosis evasion genes in immune modulation, additional studies in genetically engineered mouse models with concomitant loss of KRAS, STK11 and KEAP1 would be interesting to establish the anti-tumor immune response of SCD1 inhibition alone or combined with immunotherapy in co-mutant LUAD.
